questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Normal reaction and limiting friction on a rough incline

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Direct resolution perpendicular to slope and calculation of limiting friction F = mu R

hints: Resolve perpendicular to the plane to find $R = mg\cos\theta$, then calculate $F_{\text{lim}} = \mu R$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve perpendicular to the plane to find the normal reaction $R$:
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 5(10)\cos 30^\circ = 50\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 25\sqrt{3} \approx 43.3\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum available limiting friction force using $F_{\text{lim}} = \mu R$:
$$F_{\text{lim}} = 0.25(43.301) = 10.825 \approx 10.8\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Always find the normal reaction first by balancing forces into the plane:
$$R = 5 \times 10 \times \cos 30^\circ = 43.3\text{ N}$$

Once $R$ is known, limiting friction is simply $\mu R$:
$$F_{\text{lim}} = 0.25 \times 43.3 = 10.8\text{ N}$$
This represents the maximum grip before the block can slip.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to the plane to obtain $R = 5(10)\cos 30^\circ = 43.3\text{ N}$.
Applies $F_{\text{lim}} = \mu R = 0.25(43.301) = 10.8\text{ N}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Particle sliding down a rough inclined plane

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 2: Sliding down a rough slope with friction opposing the motion up the slope

hints: Because the particle slides down the plane, friction acts up the plane with magnitude $F = \mu R = \mu mg\cos 25^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate normal reaction and friction acting up the plane:
$$R = 4(10)\cos 25^\circ = 36.252\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.30(36.252) = 10.876 \approx 10.9\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law down the plane:
$$mg\sin 25^\circ - F = ma$$
$$4(10)\sin 25^\circ - 10.876 = 4a$$
$$16.905 - 10.876 = 6.029 = 4a \implies a = 1.507 \approx 1.50\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Friction opposes the downward slide, so it pulls up the slope:
$$F = 0.30 \times (4 \times 10 \times \cos 25^\circ) = 10.9\text{ N}$$

The net driving force is gravity down the slope minus friction up the slope:
$$a = \frac{40\sin 25^\circ - 10.88}{4} = 1.50\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates friction force $F = \mu mg\cos 25^\circ = 0.30(4)(10)\cos 25^\circ = 10.9\text{ N}$.
Applies N2L down the plane $4(10)\sin 25^\circ - 10.876 = 4a$ to obtain $a = 1.50\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Particle projected up a rough incline

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 3: Particle projected up a rough plane where both gravity and friction act downwards

hints: When moving up the plane, both the component of gravity $mg\sin\theta$ and friction $F$ act down the plane, so their effects add together.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate normal reaction and friction:
$$R = 0.8(10)\cos 10^\circ = 7.8785\text{ N}$$
$$F = 0.40(7.8785) = 3.1514\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law along the plane taking upwards as positive:
$$-mg\sin 10^\circ - F = ma$$
$$-0.8(10)\sin 10^\circ - 3.1514 = 0.8a$$
$$-1.3892 - 3.1514 = -4.5406 = 0.8a \implies a = -5.676\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
$$\text{Deceleration magnitude} = 5.68\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Since the particle is traveling up, friction pulls backwards down the plane:
$$F = 0.40 \times (8\cos 10^\circ) = 3.15\text{ N}$$

Both weight and friction work together to slow the particle down:
$$\text{Deceleration} = \frac{1.39 + 3.15}{0.8} = 5.68\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to find $R = 0.8(10)\cos 10^\circ = 7.878\text{ N}$ and friction $F = 0.40(7.878) = 3.151\text{ N}$.
Forms equation of motion $-0.8(10)\sin 10^\circ - 3.151 = 0.8a$ to find deceleration magnitude $5.68\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Deducing the coefficient of friction from observed acceleration

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 4: Using equation of motion along the plane to find F, then mu = F / R

hints: Use the equation of motion down the plane to solve for the friction force $F$, then divide by $R = mg\cos 30^\circ$ to find $\mu$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply Newton's second law down the plane to determine the friction force $F$:
$$mg\sin 30^\circ - F = ma$$
$$8(10)(0.5) - F = 8(2.4)$$
$$40 - F = 19.2 \implies F = 20.8\text{ N}$$

Resolve perpendicular to the plane to find $R$ and evaluate $\mu = \frac{F}{R}$:
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 8(10)\cos 30^\circ = 69.282\text{ N}$$
$$\mu = \frac{20.8}{69.282} \approx 0.300$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Without friction the block would accelerate at $5\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Since it only accelerates at $2.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$, friction supplies the missing force:
$$F = 40 - 8(2.4) = 20.8\text{ N}$$

Divide friction by the normal reaction to get the coefficient:
$$\mu = \frac{20.8}{80\cos 30^\circ} = \frac{20.8}{69.3} = 0.300$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies N2L down the plane $8(10)\sin 30^\circ - F = 8(2.4)$ to obtain friction force $F = 20.8\text{ N}$.
Divides by normal reaction $R = 8(10)\cos 30^\circ = 69.282\text{ N}$ to obtain $\mu = 0.300$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Pulling up a rough slope at constant speed

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 5: Constant speed motion up a rough slope (equilibrium along the slope)

hints: Constant speed means acceleration is zero, so the pulling force $P$ exactly balances the sum of the downhill gravity component and friction.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate normal reaction $R$ and friction force $F$:
$$R = mg\cos 20^\circ = 6(10)\cos 20^\circ = 56.382\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.35(56.382) = 19.734\text{ N}$$

Balance forces parallel to the plane for constant speed ($a = 0$):
$$P = mg\sin 20^\circ + F$$
$$P = 6(10)\sin 20^\circ + 19.734 = 20.521 + 19.734 = 40.255 \approx 40.3\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
When moving at steady speed up the incline, pulling force $P$ must overcome two opposing resistances:
$$R = 60\cos 20^\circ = 56.4\text{ N}, \quad F = 0.35(56.4) = 19.7\text{ N}$$

Add downhill weight and friction together to find $P$:
$$P = 60\sin 20^\circ + 19.7 = 20.5 + 19.7 = 40.3\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates normal reaction $R = 6(10)\cos 20^\circ = 56.38\text{ N}$ and friction $F = 0.35(56.38) = 19.73\text{ N}$.
Equates forces along the plane for constant speed: $P = 6(10)\sin 20^\circ + 19.73 = 40.3\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:

Calculate the magnitude of the friction force using $F = \mu R$:
$$F = 0.20(55.54) = 11.108 \approx 11.1\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Do not simply write $R = mg\cos\theta$! The angled pull provides an upward lift:
$$R = 100\cos 30^\circ - 120\sin 15^\circ = 86.6 - 31.1 = 55.5\text{ N}$$

Because normal reaction is smaller, friction is reduced as well:
$$F = 0.20 \times 55.5 = 11.1\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to plane: $R + 120\sin 15^\circ = 10(10)\cos 30^\circ$ to find $R = 55.5\text{ N}$.

$$10 - 5.993 = 4.007 = 2a \implies a = 2.0035 \approx 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
The weight provides $10\text{ N}$ driving downhill while friction holds it back with $6.0\text{ N}$:
$$F = 0.346 \times (20\cos 30^\circ) \approx 6.0\text{ N}$$

The net force is $4.0\text{ N}$, yielding the required acceleration:
$$a = \frac{10 - 6}{2} = 2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Kinematics along slope using v^2 = u^2 + 2as and v = u + at

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Rope tension up slope and work against friction

hints: The rope must overcome both the backward slope component of gravity $12g\sin 20^\circ$ and friction $F$, while also accelerating the mass: $T - mg\sin 20^\circ - F = ma$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply Newton's second law parallel to the slope:
$$T - mg\sin 20^\circ - F = ma$$
$$T - 12(10)\sin 20^\circ - 45.105 = 12(2.0)$$
$$T - 41.042 - 45.105 = 24$$

Solve for the rope tension $T$:
$$T = 24 + 86.147 = 110.147 \approx 110\text{ N}$$

Calculate the work done against friction over $5.0\text{ m}$:
$$W = F \times d = 45.105 \times 5.0 = 225.525 \approx 226\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Tension must overcome both gravity down the slope ($41.0\text{ N}$) and friction ($45.1\text{ N}$):
$$T = ma + mg\sin 20^\circ + F = 24 + 41.0 + 45.1 = 110\text{ N}$$

Work done against friction is simply force times distance along the slope:
$$W = 45.1 \times 5.0 = 226\text{ J}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies N2L up the slope $T - F - 12(10)\sin 20^\circ = 12(2.0)$.
Solves for rope tension $T = 24 + 45.10 + 41.04 = 110\text{ N}$.
Calculates work done against friction $W = F \times d = 45.10 \times 5.0 = 226\text{ J}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Core Medium: Particle projected up a rough slope, stopping, and assessing return slide

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Particle projected up rough slope with exact sin and cos ratios

hints: The angle has $\sin\alpha = 0.6$ and $\cos\alpha = 0.8$.
While moving up, both gravity component $mg\sin\alpha$ and friction $F = \mu mg\cos\alpha$ pull down the slope.
Apply Newton's second law along the slope to find deceleration $a = 8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with final velocity $v = 0$ to find the stopping distance.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate normal reaction and friction force:
$$R = mg\cos\alpha = 0.5(10)(0.8) = 4.0\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.25(4.0) = 1.0\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law up the plane:
$$-mg\sin\alpha - F = ma$$
$$-0.5(10)(0.6) - 1.0 = 0.5a$$
$$-3.0 - 1.0 = -4.0 = 0.5a \implies a = -8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
$$\text{Deceleration} = 8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Find distance traveled to instantaneous rest using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:
$$0^2 = 12^2 - 2(8.0)s$$
$$16.0s = 144 \implies s = 9.0\text{ m}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
On the way up, gravity pulls back with $3.0\text{ N}$ and friction pulls back with $1.0\text{ N}$:
$$F_{\text{net}} = -(3.0 + 1.0) = -4.0\text{ N}$$

Dividing by mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ confirms the deceleration:
$$a = \frac{-4.0}{0.5} = -8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Use the stopping formula to find the apex distance:
$$s = \frac{u^2}{2|a|} = \frac{144}{16} = 9.0\text{ m}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to find $R = 0.5(10)(0.8) = 4.0\text{ N}$ and friction $F = 0.25(4.0) = 1.0\text{ N}$.
Applies N2L up the plane $-0.5(10)(0.6) - 1.0 = 0.5a$ to show deceleration is $8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Uses $0^2 = 12^2 - 2(8.0)s$ to obtain distance $s = 9.0\text{ m}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Checking whether particle remains at rest at apex by comparing mg sin alpha with limiting friction

hints: At the highest point, the tendency of motion is downwards.
Compare the downhill component of gravity $mg\sin\alpha$ with the maximum available friction $F_{\text{lim}} = \mu R$.
If $mg\sin\alpha > F_{\text{lim}}$, the particle will slide down; then apply N2L down the plane.

walkthrough.text:
Compare the downhill gravity force with limiting friction:
$$mg\sin\alpha = 0.5(10)(0.6) = 3.0\text{ N}$$
$$F_{\text{lim}} = 1.0\text{ N}$$
Since $3.0\text{ N} > 1.0\text{ N}$, the downhill gravity overcomes limiting friction, so the particle does not remain at rest; it slides down.

Apply Newton's second law down the plane with friction acting up the plane:
$$mg\sin\alpha - F = ma$$
$$3.0 - 1.0 = 0.5a \implies 2.0 = 0.5a \implies a = 4.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
At instantaneous rest, gravity wants to pull the particle down with $3.0\text{ N}$, while maximum grip is only $1.0\text{ N}$:
$$3.0\text{ N} > 1.0\text{ N} \implies \text{the particle slips downwards}$$

On the descent, friction flips direction to resist the fall:
$$a = \frac{3.0 - 1.0}{0.5} = 4.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Compares downhill gravity component $mg\sin\alpha = 3.0\text{ N}$ with $F_{\text{lim}} = 1.0\text{ N}$ to conclude the particle slides down.
Applies N2L down the plane $3.0 - 1.0 = 0.5a$ to obtain acceleration $a = 4.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Find normal reaction $R = 4g\cos 30^\circ = 34.641\text{ N}$ and friction $F = 8.660\text{ N}$.
Apply Newton's second law for the first stage: $P - mg\sin 30^\circ - F = 4a_1$ with $P = 50\text{ N}$.
Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2a_1 s$ with $u = 0$ and $s = 6.0\text{ m}$ to find speed at point $B$.

$$F = \mu R = 0.25(34.641) = 8.660\text{ N}$$

Apply Newton's second law up the plane for stage 1:
$$P - mg\sin 30^\circ - F = ma_1$$
$$50 - 4(10)(0.5) - 8.660 = 4a_1$$
$$50 - 20 - 8.660 = 21.340 = 4a_1 \implies a_1 = 5.335\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Calculate the speed at point $B$ using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:

teacher_walkthrough.text:
During the pull, $50\text{ N}$ overcomes downhill gravity ($20\text{ N}$) and friction ($8.66\text{ N}$):
$$F_{\text{net}} = 50 - 20 - 8.66 = 21.34\text{ N}$$
$$a_1 = \frac{21.34}{4} = 5.335\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

From rest over $6.0\text{ m}$, the speed at $B$ is:

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Forming equations of motion and proving acceleration for connected particles on rough incline

hints: Given $\tan\theta = 0.75$, the angle corresponds to a 3-4-5 triangle with $\sin\theta = 0.6$ and $\cos\theta = 0.8$.
Resolve perpendicular to the incline for particle $A$: $R = 2g\cos\theta = 16\text{ N}$, giving friction $F = 0.25(16) = 4.0\text{ N}$.
Write the equation of motion for $A$ moving up the incline: $T - 2g\sin\theta - F = 2a$.
Write the equation of motion for $B$ descending vertically: $3g - T = 3a$, then eliminate $T$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate normal reaction and friction force on particle $A$:
$$R = m_A g\cos\theta = 2(10)(0.8) = 16\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.25(16) = 4.0\text{ N}$$

Set up equations of motion for both particles:
$$\text{For } A \text{ (up slope)}: \quad T - 2(10)(0.6) - 4.0 = 2a \implies T - 16.0 = 2a$$
$$\text{For } B \text{ (downwards)}: \quad 3(10) - T = 3a \implies 30 - T = 3a$$

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$ and solve for acceleration $a$:
$$(T - 16.0) + (30 - T) = 2a + 3a$$
$$14.0 = 5a \implies a = \frac{14.0}{5} = 2.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
First identify all resistances on particle $A$: downhill weight is $12\text{ N}$ and friction is $4\text{ N}$, totaling $16\text{ N}$ opposing motion:
$$R = 20(0.8) = 16\text{ N}, \quad F = 0.25(16) = 4.0\text{ N}$$

Hanging mass $B$ pulls with $30\text{ N}$, leaving a net driving force of $14\text{ N}$ across the total mass ($5\text{ kg}$):
$$a = \frac{30 - 16}{2 + 3} = \frac{14}{5} = 2.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Finds normal reaction $R = 2(10)(0.8) = 16\text{ N}$ and friction $F = 0.25(16) = 4.0\text{ N}$ on particle $A$.
Sets up equations of motion: $T - 2(10)(0.6) - 4.0 = 2a$ and $3(10) - T = 3a$.
Adds equations to show $5a = 14 \implies a = 2.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

hints: Particle $ descends  = 1.8	ext{ m}$ vertically from rest with constant acceleration  = 2.8	ext{ m s}^{-2}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Further distance moved by particle A after string becomes slack until rest

hints: Once $B$ hits the ground, the string goes slack, so $T = 0$.
Particle $A$ continues moving up the plane with initial speed $u = 3.1749\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Opposing forces are downhill gravity $12\text{ N}$ and friction $4\text{ N}$, giving deceleration $a_{\text{slack}} = -8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Calculate further distance $s_2 = \frac{u^2}{2|a|}$, then add the initial $1.8\text{ m}$ to find total distance traveled up the plane.

walkthrough.text:
Apply Newton's second law to particle $A$ with $T = 0$:
$$-m_A g\sin\theta - F = m_A a_{\text{slack}}$$
$$-12 - 4.0 = 2a_{\text{slack}} \implies -16 = 2a_{\text{slack}} \implies a_{\text{slack}} = -8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
$$\text{Deceleration magnitude} = 8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Calculate further distance $s_2$ traveled up the plane to instantaneous rest:
$$0^2 = 3.1749^2 - 2(8.0)s_2$$
$$16s_2 = 10.08 \implies s_2 = \frac{10.08}{16} = 0.63\text{ m}$$

Calculate the total distance particle $A$ has traveled up the plane from its starting position:
$$s_{\text{total}} = s_1 + s_2 = 1.8 + 0.63 = 2.43\text{ m}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
When the string goes slack, $A$ coasts under gravity and friction alone:
$$a_{\text{slack}} = \frac{-(12 + 4)}{2} = -8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

The particle travels an extra $0.63\text{ m}$ before stopping:
$$s_2 = \frac{10.08}{2(8)} = 0.63\text{ m}$$
Adding the $1.8\text{ m}$ traveled before impact gives total distance $2.43\text{ m}$.
